maths_errors.text: 'Both happen' = multiply. 'Either happens' = add. The words tell you which rule to use.
maths_errors.correction: The word 'or' alone does not tell you to add. Simple addition only works when the events are mutually exclusive. Example: flip a coin and roll a die. P(head or 6) = 1/2 + 1/6 − 1/12 = 7/12, not 1/2 + 1/6 = 2/3. Likewise, 'and' means P(A) × P(B) only for independent events. The lesson's own next mistake (slides[3].mistakes[1]) contradicts this sentence.

maths_errors.text: If the question says 'both', 'and', or involves two separate trials (two coins, two dice), multiply the probabilities.
maths_errors.correction: Multiplying gives the probability of one particular combined outcome only. Some questions about two trials need more than this. Example: P(one head and one tail from two coins) = 1/2 × 1/2 + 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/2, not 1/4. Example: P(at least one 6 from two dice) = 1 − (5/6)² = 11/36. For dependent events, the second probability must be the conditional one, not P(B).

missing_spec_content.spec_text: calculate the probability of independent and dependent combined events, including using tree diagrams and other representations
missing_spec_content.why: Dependent events (for example, picking without replacement) are not taught at all. Tree diagrams are also absent.

The lesson never says what assumptions lie behind its calculations. Examples are fair or equally likely outcomes, independence of trials, and replacement or non-replacement. The independence assumption is not discussed as an assumption.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: including knowing when to add and when to multiply two or more probabilities
missing_spec_content.why: Only two events are covered. Combining three or more probabilities is not taught. Combining multiply-then-add (for example, summing the branches of a tree) is not taught either.

above_gcse.text: Warning: the OR rule P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B) is the general version; the simpler addition only works when A and B cannot both happen.
above_gcse.why: The given spec sections do not require the general addition law as a formula. GCSE normally handles overlapping events by counting in a Venn diagram or sample space. Here it is given with no example, so it may confuse a first-time learner.

density.text: The rule you use depends on the relationship between the events: if two events cannot happen at the same time they are mutually exclusive (e.g. rolling a 3 and rolling a 5 on one die), and you add their probabilities. If two events don't affect each other they are independent (e.g. flipping a coin and rolling a die), and you multiply their probabilities.
density.why: The first sentence defines mutually exclusive, gives an example and states the add rule, all after a colon. The next sentence does the same for independent events. That is four new ideas in two long sentences.

density.text: Independent events — AND rule: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B)  |  Mutually exclusive events — OR rule: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B)
density.why: Two different rules with two different conditions are packed onto one line, separated only by '|'.

density.text: Warning: the OR rule P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B) is the general version; the simpler addition only works when A and B cannot both happen.
density.why: It introduces a new formula with a new term, P(A and B) for events that are not independent. It gives no reason for the subtraction and no example.

The instruction says 'Draw the sample space', but a list split by '|' is shown instead of a grid. The meaning of '|' is not explained. This also contradicts the lesson's own advice to draw a grid rather than list outcomes.

density.text: Using the OR rule P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) when the events are not mutually exclusive — double-counting outcomes that are in both events.
density.why: It does not explain why adding double-counts. There is no example of an outcome that lies in both events.
